title: Relative clauses 1: clauses with who/that/which
subtitle: the woman who lives next door
summary: Use who or that for people and that or which for things to say which person or thing you mean.

lesson.heading: What is a relative clause?
lesson.text: A clause is a part of a sentence. Last week we had a party and a lot of people came. Everybody enjoyed it. In one sentence: *Everybody **who came to the party** enjoyed it.* A relative clause tells us **which** person or thing (or what kind of person or thing) the speaker means.

examples.text: the woman **who lives next door to me**
examples.note: 'who lives next door to me' tells us which woman
'who complain all the time' tells us what kind of people

lesson.heading: who for people
lesson.text: We use **who** in a relative clause for people, not for things.

examples.text: The woman **who lives** next door to me is a doctor.
I don't like people **who complain** all the time.
An architect is someone **who designs** buildings.
What was the name of the person **who called**?
Do you know anyone **who wants** to buy a car?

lesson.heading: that for people too
lesson.text: We can also use **that** for people. But we never use **which** for people.

examples.text: The woman **that lives** next door to me is a doctor.
Do you know the person **that took** these pictures?

left.label: people: who / that
examples: The driver **who** caused the accident was fined.
The waiter **that** served us was impolite.
The people **who** were arrested have now been released.

right.label: things: that / which
right.text: Never who. That is usually more natural than which.
examples: I don't like stories **that** have unhappy endings.
Grace works for a company **which** makes furniture.
The machine **that** broke down is working again now.

lesson.heading: Don't add he/she/they/it
lesson.text: In relative clauses we use **who/that/which** instead of *he/she/they/it* - we do not use both.

examples.text: I met a Canadian woman **who is** an English teacher.
examples.note: two sentences: I met a Canadian woman. She is an English teacher.

examples.text: Where are the keys **that were** on the table?
examples.wrong: the keys they were on the table

lesson.heading: what = the thing(s) that
lesson.text: **What** means *the thing that*. After **everything**, **the machine** and other nouns we use **that**, not what.

examples.text: The machine **that broke down** is now working again.

lesson.text: Test it: if the relative clause answers 'which one?', keep who/that/which - and never follow a noun with what.

exercises.prompt: An architect is someone ___ designs buildings.
exercises.explanation: An architect is a person, so we use who (or that), never which.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its definition. Every definition begins with 'someone who ...'.

pairs.right: someone who buys something from a shop
someone who breaks into a house to steal things
someone who pays rent to live somewhere
someone who doesn't tell the truth
someone who expects the worst to happen

exercises.prompt: A girl was injured in the accident. She is now in hospital. Make one sentence.
exercises.answer: The girl who was injured in the accident is now in hospital
exercises.explanation: The relative clause 'who was injured in the accident' tells us which girl.

exercises.prompt: A waiter served us. He was impolite and impatient. The waiter ___ served us was impolite and impatient.
exercises.explanation: A waiter is a person: who or that, not which.

exercises.prompt: A building was destroyed in the fire. The building ___ was destroyed in the fire has now been rebuilt.
exercises.explanation: A building is a thing, so we use that or which, never who.
A shop is a thing, so we use that (or which), not who or what.

exercises.statement: What was the name of the person who phoned?
exercises.explanation: Correct. Person is a people word, so who is right.

exercises.statement: I don't like stories who have unhappy endings.
exercises.explanation: I don't like stories that have unhappy endings. We do not use who for things.

exercises.prompt: It seems that Earth is the only planet ___ life.
exercises.explanation: A planet is a thing, so the relative pronoun is that or which.

exercises.statement: Dan said some things about me they were not true.
exercises.explanation: Dan said some things about me that were not true. Use that instead of they, not both.

exercises.prompt: We live in a world ___ changing all the time.
exercises.explanation: After a noun (a world) we use that or which - never what.
After everything we use that, not what.
